Calling this a “flying car” is a rather generous interpretation of what appears to be a highly choreographed engineering demonstration.
McMurtry’s Spéirling had already demonstrated upside-down driving using fan-generated suction, producing up to 2,000 kg of downforce. That is genuine engineering, but suction that holds a vehicle against a surface is fundamentally different from propulsion that lifts it into the air.
As for the Roadster’s thrusters, the real questions are vehicle mass, thrust-to-weight ratio, stability, control, flight duration, passenger safety and whether the demonstration can be independently reproduced with a production-spec vehicle. A spectacular launch, mid-air manoeuvre and soft landing do not answer any of these questions. Nor does a video establish the vehicle’s actual configuration or whether it can carry passengers during such manoeuvres.
And this is where the credibility gap matters. The Roadster was announced in 2017, endured years of delays, and is now being presented with yet another extraordinary set of claims. The latest reports still point to production in 2028.
Tesla has every right to push engineering boundaries. But innovation should be measured by reproducible results, engineering transparency and delivery, not by how spectacularly a prototype performs in a launch presentation.
Until Tesla demonstrates sustained, controlled flight with a fully documented, production-representative vehicle, I would call this an impressive prototype demonstration, not proof that a commercially viable flying car exists.
The technology deserves scrutiny, not blind applause. And after nearly nine years of waiting for the Roadster, scepticism is entirely justified.
